name: Bemotrizinol

lead: Bemotrizinol is an oil-soluble sunscreen filter that covers both UVB and UVA and is very photostable, so protection holds through the day. Skincare enthusiasts seek it out in EU, Australian and Asian products to limit photoaging and pigmentation.

It absorbs UV across about 280-400 nm, converts it to heat and helps stabilise filters like avobenzone. It has been approved in the EU since 2000. Wikipedia reports an FDA announcement of approval for US sunscreens on 9 June 2026.

paras: It is used in daily sunscreens, often imported or chosen from non-US brands, and blended with other filters.
Registered trials of a 6% sunscreen examined absorption, phototoxicity, photoallergy and irritation. Lab studies found no estrogenic activity, and aquatic toxicity studies exist.

angle.text: Bemotrizinol is a photostable UVA and UVB filter, so the sunscreen keeps working through the day and less photoaging and pigmentation builds up. Support comes from sunscreen testing and long regional use.

lead: Bemotrizinol (INCI: bis-ethylhexyloxyphenol methoxyphenyl triazine, BEMT; trade names Tinosorb S, Escalol S and Parsol Shield) is an oil-soluble organic UV filter used in sunscreens and SPF moisturisers. People use sunscreens containing it to protect skin from the UV exposure that drives tanning, sunburn, uneven pigmentation and photoaging, so the complexion keeps its tone and texture over the years [1][2][3].

It absorbs across the UVB and UVA ranges, with absorption peaks near 310 and 340 nm, and is notable for staying intact under sunlight. It is also used to stabilise less stable filters such as avobenzone [2][4]. Stanford Medicine coverage points to two practical differences from older US filters: protection that extends to 400 nm, where existing US filters reach about 370 nm, and a lightweight feel with no white cast, unlike mineral sunscreens [5].

Bemotrizinol has been approved in the European Union since 2000 and in Australia, and is widely used in European and Asian sunscreens. It was long absent from US products because it was not in the FDA's sunscreen monograph. Wikipedia reports an FDA announcement approving it for US sunscreens in June 2026, and news coverage that summer described it as the first new US sunscreen filter in roughly two decades [2][5][6][7].

Human studies include a series of registered 2020 to 2022 trials of a 6% bemotrizinol sunscreen covering absorption, phototoxicity, photoallergy and irritation, plus older European studies of multi-filter sunscreens containing it [8][9][10][11][12][13].
infobox: Tinosorb S, Tinosorb S Aqua, Escalol S, Parsol Shield
FDA approval for sunscreens announced June 2026 at 6% (per Wikipedia and Stanford Medicine coverage)

paras: Bemotrizinol appears in face and body sunscreens, daily SPF moisturisers, tinted products and make-up with SPF, where it supplies broad UVA and UVB coverage without an inorganic white film. Stanford dermatologists interviewed in 2026 described the lack of white cast and the non-greasy finish as practical advantages over mineral filters and over older chemical filters that need oily stabilisers [5].

Photoprotection matters for appearance because UV exposure contributes to tanning, hyperpigmentation and visible photoaging. Dermatologists quoted by Stanford noted that people with pigment conditions such as melasma may still use tinted mineral sunscreens for visible-light coverage, with one, Zakia Rahman, advising people not to discard them [5].
A water-phase version, Tinosorb S Aqua, embeds the compound in a PMMA matrix dispersed in water so that formulators can add it to light, water-based textures [2].

Bemotrizinol is a symmetric 1,3,5-triazine bearing two ethylhexyloxy-hydroxyphenyl groups and a methoxyphenyl group, formula C38H49N3O5. It is a large, highly lipophilic molecule that dissolves in oils and not in water [1][2].

It takes up UV photons and returns the energy as heat through rapid non-radiative decay rather than forming reactive by-products, which is why it is described as photostable: about 98.4% remains intact after 50 minimal erythemal doses of UV [2]. It has been shown to act as a photostabiliser for retinyl palmitate combinations and for avobenzone, and reports describe SPF synergy with bisoctrizole, ethylhexyl triazone and iscotrizinol [2][14].

An in vitro ranking of EU-authorised filters at their maximum permitted concentrations placed bemotrizinol first by SPF contribution, according to Wikipedia [2]. A 2025 review of US sunscreen regulation grouped it with bisoctrizole, drometrizole trisiloxane and terephthalylidene dicamphor sulfonic acid as newer filters used abroad that offer broader and more stable protection, and argued that wider access could help reduce UV-related skin cancer [3].

Laboratory work has examined it in nanostructured lipid carriers, nanoemulsions and sprayable emulsions for penetration and photostability [15][4]. Stanford dermatologist Susan Swetter described it as the best broad-spectrum UV filter available, in an interview published in 2026 [5].

Because the molecule is large, researchers quoted by Stanford Medicine said it is minimally absorbed through skin, and that animal studies showed no increased cancer risk or endocrine disruption; human testing of a 6% concentration found no concerning irritation [5]. Wikipedia reports that in vitro and rat uterotrophic assays found no estrogenic activity, in contrast to some other organic filters [2].

A Phase 3 maximal-usage pharmacokinetic trial of a 6% bemotrizinol sunscreen enrolled 162 participants, preceded by a 14-person Phase 1 absorption study. Separate registered trials assessed photoallergy (n=50), phototoxicity (n=34) and irritation, sensitisation and cumulative irritation (n=224). The registry entries do not publish outcomes [8][9][10][11][12].

Bemotrizinol was one of ten filters tested on brine shrimp and marine microalgae in a 2020 study, and triazine UV filters were identified as pollutants in indoor dust and air in South China [16][17]. Stanford experts said they knew of no evidence that it harms the environment and noted that the term reef safe has no standardised regulatory definition [5].

The registered 6% bemotrizinol programme comprised: a Phase 1 pharmacokinetic study begun in November 2020 (14 participants), a Phase 3 maximal-usage trial begun in March 2022 (162), and Phase 2 trials on photoallergy (50), phototoxicity (34) and dermal irritation, sensitisation and cumulative irritation (224) in early 2022 [8][9][10][11][12].

A 2008 single-centre, open, placebo-controlled intra-individual study tested a very-high-protection sunscreen containing bemotrizinol (Tinosorb S), Tinosorb M and avobenzone in 12 patients with polymorphic light eruption. In 10 patients the eruption could be provoked on placebo-treated skin; on the sunscreen-treated forearm none developed it [13]. A 2015 study of retinyl palmitate formulations found that bemotrizinol reduced the in vitro phototoxicity of one combination with avobenzone and that clinical photopatch tests showed no phototoxic or photoallergenic reactions [14].
A 2012 trial of UV and UV-visible light photoprotection in melasma (68 participants) and a European photopatch study (about 1,000 participants) concern sunscreens more broadly [18][19].

Bemotrizinol, sold by BASF as Tinosorb S, has been approved in the EU since 2000; it is also approved in Australia and used across Asia [2][2]. In the United States, new filters must pass through FDA's OTC monograph process, and a 2025 review attributed the long gap to regulatory inertia, noting that the new OTC Monograph Order Request pathway might change that [3].

Wikipedia reports a June 2026 FDA press release approving bemotrizinol for sunscreens; Stanford Medicine described it in August 2026 as approved at 6% for adults and for children from six months, with DSM-Firmenich holding exclusive US marketing rights for 18 months and products expected that September [2][5]. Editorials in Annals of Internal Medicine and The Medical Letter appeared in 2026 [20][21]. A press release states that Ultra Violette was the first brand to launch a US sunscreen with the filter [22].

The approval drew coverage in Vogue, local television and on Hacker News, where it was framed as the arrival in the US of an ingredient used in Europe and Asia for years [6][7][23]. Stanford noted that bemotrizinol products were already available to US shoppers from overseas retailers before the approval [5].

timeline.event: Approved for use in the European Union [2].
Phase 1 absorption study of a 6% sunscreen begins [9].
Phase 3 maximal-usage and Phase 2 safety trials of 6% bemotrizinol begin [8][10][11][12].
Review argues newer filters such as bemotrizinol should be made available in the US [3].
FDA approval for sunscreen use announced (June); first US products launch later that year [2][5][22].
